# Changing Higher Education in the United Kingdom: Examining Three Trends through a Neoliberal Lens
**Amy Perry***
VER ROUGHLY THE PAST HALF CENTURY, HIGHER EDUCATION IN the United Kingdom has experienced a rather dramatic shift in response to national and global forces. Once positioned as the site for the creation of cultural goods, it has since been recast as a factory and its principal product is the added value (in the form of human capital) that students receive as they are processed along the conveyor belt and handed their degrees. In large part, this change can be attributed to the ascent of neoliberalism both in the United Kingdom and globally. The beginning of the current political era is often marked by Margaret Thatcher's election to prime minister, although the seeds of neoliberalism predate her election. While Thatcher successfully targeted and dismantled a number of institutions formed in the post-war Keynesian era, education was never a primary target of Thatcher's government. Nonetheless, both during and after Thatcher's tenure as prime minister, higher education was subject to a number of trends and forces that altered the way higher education looks in the United Kingdom today.
The purpose of this article is twofold: to provide a brief historical overview of the ascent of neoliberalism in the United Kingdom and to examine three trends in higher education through a neoliberal lens—the widening of participation and the politics of aspiration, the emergence of the student entrepreneur-consumer, and the marketization of higher education. The article also explores the use of online courses as a response to market pressures and the potential impact on students.
^(* )AMY PERRY (amynperry1984@gmail.com) holds a PhD in Sociology from the University of California, Riverside. Her research focuses on gender, race, immigration, and political discourse.
## **Neoliberalism's Rise: The Election of Margaret Thatcher**
Neoliberalism is often used as a buzzword with a range that may extend beyond its reach. Among researchers, there is no consensus on the principles that the term neoliberalism is supposed to embody. Broadly speaking, neoliberalism refers to an economic theory that champions the role of free market forces in state governance, with a rhetorical emphasis on individual freedom (Peck & Tickell 2007). The flexibility and generality of the term has led some to question its theoretical utility, but to the extent that there is a distinctive philosophical, political, and economic movement that we call neoliberalism, it is in part the flexibility and generality of its principles that has fueled the movement's staying power (Schmidt & Thatcher 2014). The stickiness of its rhetoric lies in the appeal of its central concepts: individual liberty and freedom (Harvey 2007). Yet while the rhetoric of neoliberalism emphasizes a decreased role of the state, the neoliberal project involves rolling out new forms of governance more than it does rolling back the role of the state (Peck & Tickell 2007).
At times, neoliberalism is spoken of with an almost mythic reverence. Neoliberalism is the bogeyman, a top-down conspiracy theory on the part of a set of global ruling elites. In actuality, however, neoliberalism did not experience a global, unified rollout but rather developed in myriad localized settings before it took on global import as a loosely grouped set of general governing principles (Peck & Tickell 2007, Schmidt & Thatcher 2014). Neoliberalism was a response to, and the result of, global forces, crises, and events such as the energy crisis of the early 1970s, but the ways in which it took root and the paths it took to prominence varied from nation to nation and depended on a combination of global and local concerns. In the United Kingdom, neoliberalism followed a monetarist path as a reaction to and attempt to combat inflation and rising prices (Harvey 2007).
### *Neoliberalism and Thatcherism*
Neoliberalism arose in the 1970s and 1980s as a reaction against the perceived failing of the so-called welfarism of Keynesian economics (Kendall 2003). The election of world leaders like Margaret Thatcher as prime minister of the United Kingdom and Ronald Reagan as president of the United States are frequently cited as evidence of a paradigm shift away from Keynesian economics and toward a focus on (or fixation with) free market ideology, but the ideological seeds that gave rise to neoliberalism predate the elections of Thatcher and Reagan. Certain core elements of neoliberal thought
date back to the nineteenth century, such as the emphasis on individualism and the idea of self-made men in Victorian England (Littler 2013). This is not to suggest a direct line between neoliberalism and Victorian morality—self-care may have instead fertilized the ground in which neoliberalism took root—but rather that neoliberalism did not come to prominence as an entirely novel theory or philosophy and shares some similarities with this earlier English tradition.
More direct links to neoliberalism's lineage can be found in German ordoliberalism and Chicago School economics in the United States (Kendall 2003). In the early 1970s, US economists attempted to revive Chile's economy following Augusto Pinochet's coup by successfully implementing policies that, among other initiatives, strengthened the role of the market and privatized public assets (Harvey 2007). This success, however, was largely restricted to ruling elites and foreign investors (Harvey 2007), a pattern that to a certain extent held true for the Chicago School's neoliberal successors.
Neoliberalism in the United Kingdom and elsewhere gained prominence as a reaction to the myriad economic and social crises of the time. In the early 1970s, economic instability in many parts of the world created an environment ripe for the ascent of neoliberalism (Fourcade-Gourinchas & Babb 2002). The growing discontent and interest in socialism that accompanied the precarious economy posed a threat to ruling elites (Harvey 2007). Through privatization, financialization, state redistribution, and crisis manipulation and management, neoliberal practices enabled ruling elites to resecure class power (Harvey 2007). State governments varied in how they rationalized the implementation of neoliberal state policies, with some, like the United Kingdom, leaning heavily on domestic concerns (Fourcade-Gourinchas & Babb 2002). International organizations such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) have played a prominent role in scattering the seeds of neoliberal ideology globally (Harvey 2007).
Amidst a decade of turmoil, Margaret Thatcher became the leader of the embattled Conservative Party in 1975 (Scott-Samuel et al. 2014) and in 1979 she was elected prime minister of the United Kingdom. Thatcher's aggressive support of neoliberal policies went above and beyond her US partner in crime Ronald Reagan (Harvey 2007). Her stringent support for neoliberal policies stood in contrast to the U-turn of former Prime Minister Edward Heath (1970–1974), who was also with the Conservative Party (Scott-Samuel et al. 2014, 55). Thatcher's rise to power was a reaction to the perceived inadequacies of Heath's time as prime minister, yet even so, Thatcher's tenure was, to an extent, stymied by opposition within her own
party, and her vision for the United Kingdom was never fully realized, as she found herself unable to dismantle key institutions of the welfare state such as the National Health Service (Harvey 2007). Thatcher was nonetheless broadly successful in achieving her aims. As a fierce champion of the free market, Thatcher oversaw the growth of business interests in the United Kingdom and successfully chipped away at other elements of the welfare state (Scott-Samuel et al. 2014). As a political ethos, Thatcherism consisted of three major elements: monetarism and privatization, decreased union standing, and anti-socialism (Edwards 1989).
During the early part of Thatcher's reign, education was not targeted for radical restructuring like other key institutions. While education as a whole underwent a sort of "creeping privatization," higher education in particular did not experience significant privatization (Whitty & Menter 1989, 44). Universities did see a significant slash in state funding in the form of stateprovided research grants and direct grants (Edwards 1989). Arguably the most significant change to higher education during Thatcher's reign came in the form of the Education Reform Act of 1988, which generated sweeping changes at all levels of education, abolishing tenure for incoming faculty and introducing market forces via expanded parental choice (Machin & Vignoles 2006). The Education Reform Act of 1988 can be attributed in part to the ascendance of the New Right as a political force in the United Kingdom, which consisted of both neoliberal and neoconservative strands (Taylor 1993) and was an uneasy blend of economic libertarianism and social and moral authoritarianism (Whitty & Menter 1989).
## **Neoliberalism and Higher Education in the United Kingdom: ** **Post-Thatcher**
Although higher education may not have been a principal target for Thatcher, she employed neoliberal logics against her chosen targets and the general tenor of her tenure as prime minister created a fertile context for the New Right to push through the 1980 and 1998 Education Reform Acts (Clay & Cole 1991). The effects of neoliberalism on higher education extended past her tenure as prime minister and into the twenty-first century. The 1998 Teaching and Education Act and the 2004 Higher Education Act both challenged the taken-for-granted norm of accessible higher education and put students in the United Kingdom on a similar level as their US counterparts in having to contend with tuition costs. The 1998 Teaching and Education Act saw an end to free higher education tuition and a reduction
in maintenance grants (Leckey & Neill 2001), while the 2004 Act extended these changes and introduced top-up fees, which allowed universities to cover budget shortfalls by increasing tuition (Stevenson et al. 2010).
Around the same time period (the late twentieth century), three post-Thatcher trends emerged: the top-down push for widening participation, the transformation of students into market agents, and the increasing marketization of higher education. The following sections explore each trend and its implications for higher education students in the United Kingdom.
### *Widening Participation*
Widening participation refers broadly to state and institutional interventions aimed at increasing participation for groups with historically low participation rates in UK higher education. Target groups for expanded participation have changed over the course of the twentieth century, but the focus has always been on underparticipating groups who are viewed as structurally or socially disadvantaged (Vignoles & Murray 2016). Widening participation initiatives often targeted potential low-income students from disadvantaged neighborhoods (Brown 2013). The government focus on widening participation has increased in the twenty-first century from a peripheral to a central concern for government officials ( Jones & Thomas 2005).
Widening participation, on one level, fits squarely within social justice discourse. Terminologically, widening participation evokes the rhetorical shift that equality discourse underwent in the late part of the twentieth century; in the United Kingdom, a so-called weak definition of equality that emphasized access and equal opportunity gave way to a so-called strong definition that emphasized participation and equal outcome (Taylor 1993). Associated terms include diversity, inclusion, and equality (Stevenson et al. 2010). The presumption that widening participation is an equalizing force consistent with social justice aims can be found in the on-the-ground understanding and use of the term by those who work within higher education institutions. For example, Stevenson et al. (2010) found in their institutional case study that staff members drew heavily on the language and logic of social justice, which suggests that perhaps what institutional actors have absorbed from widening participation rhetoric is its potential to address structural disadvantages (see also Shaw et al. 2007). Widening participation has also been advocated as a means of advancing the United Kingdom by accessing a pool of underutilized talent (Fletcher et al. 2013) and as serving the interests of individual organizations (Shaw et al. 2007). Thus, widening participation
is pitched in the abstract as advantageous at all levels of society from the state down to the citizen.
Moving beyond abstract conceptualizations of widening participation, actual policies aimed at increasing participation rates reveal a tension at the heart of the movement with regard to whose interests are advanced by these initiatives. Jones and Thomas (2005) identify two dominant strands of government policies that aim to increase higher education participation that differ principally in the extent to which they do (or do not) acknowledge the need for institutional reform in order to ensure equivalent outcomes for historically underparticipating demographic groups. The academic strand consists of those policies that aim to attract the so-called best and brightest of historically underparticipating demographic groups without positing the need for any sort of institutional reform. Underparticipation within this strand is framed as an issue of attitude, not structure, and thus the solution is to raise aspirations. The utilitarian approach, by contrast, consists of policies that cite a need for institutional reform and position both higher education institutions and participants as needing to be flexible and responsive to market forces. Neither strand of policy, according to Jones and Thomas (2005), goes far enough in fostering positive outcomes for underrepresented groups. Institutional policies are similarly lukewarm in effect; while universities have developed policies that explicitly or implicitly invoke widening participation, these policies have been unevenly developed and implemented (Fletcher et al. 2013).
It could be argued that despite the rhetoric, widening participation serves the interests of the market more than it acts as an equalizing force. To the extent that widening participation policies lean on ideas about merit and high aspiration as necessary conditions for participation and ignore structural impediments to participation, widening participation reduces underparticipation to individual failure. By stressing the role of merit, widening participation rhetoric evokes the specter of meritocracy, which serves the interests of ruling elites much more than it does the disadvantaged (Littler 2013). While the rhetoric underpinning widening participation stresses the need for higher education in order to achieve self-betterment, it inadequately addresses student access to education, and contemporaneous developments like the 1998 and 2004 Education Acts even undermine student access.
The rhetoric of aspiration similarly renders the structural as individual. As an explanation for low participation rates, it casts the disadvantaged as solely responsible for their own betterment within the structures that disadvantaged them in the first place. The politics of aspiration does little to
address how the educational system perpetuates inequalities for low-income families, and in fact implicitly frames those with minimal education (as a result of those inequalities) as responsible for their own lack of attainment (Brown 2013). In order for widening participation initiatives to be truly successful, educational interventions need to occur earlier in the pipeline (Vignoles & Murray 2016).
Aspiration rhetoric has not been restricted solely to widening participation. Following the fall from power of the Conservative Party, New Labour attempted to fundamentally reconceptualize the state relationship to the citizen by advancing a narrative of aspirational citizenship over expectational citizenship (Raco 2009). Accompanying this reconceptualization was a shift in political focus from rights-based politics to responsibilities-based politics, an emphasis on equality over equity, and a reformulation of the role of education as oriented toward individualization over socialization (Raco 2009, 438). These shifts in the narratives and the policies that accompanied them were justified on the grounds that welfare-based governmentality encourages dependence and hampers individual ability to become productive citizens (Raco 2009). It should be noted that the politics of aspiration is neither wholly nor solely a New Labour project and that an emphasis on aspiration as a key force in upward mobility transcends political party affiliation. For example, David Cameron (prime minister and conservative party member following the New Labour regime) repeatedly referred to Britain as an aspiration nation (Littler 2013).
The aspiration narrative buoys the myth of meritocracy, where the best (the most intelligent, the most capable, the most driven) should be freed from constraints such that they can reach the top while the worst are allowed to sink to the bottom (see Littler 2013 for an extended discussion of the problems with meritocracy and David Cameron's Aspiration Nation). It is free market ideology applied to the life courses of British citizens rather than goods or services.
This is not to suggest that top-down discursive projects are necessarily successful or universal; the cold logic behind aspiration conflicts with the expectations and understandings of the state-citizen relationship that British citizens carried with them through the middle part of the twentieth century. Student resistance to certain higher education initiatives suggests that perhaps the reconceptualization of citizenship from expectational to aspirational (and perhaps the attendant conceptualization of the aspirational student) is incomplete. For example, the 2010 student protests against proposals to increase tuition and abolish the Educational Maintenance Allowance relied
on a mixture of individualized rhetoric and a defense of state-supported education and citizen entitlements (Brown 2013).
Widening participation and the politics of aspiration cast higher education as the way out, but do little to address structural inequalities that place children from working-class families and racial-ethnic minorities at a disadvantage. Under neoliberalism, state citizens are responsible for their own betterment (and, conversely, for their own failure). This is perhaps one of the more insidious consequences of the neoliberal logic that state officials employ in justifying particular acts of governance; it elides the state's culpability in structural disadvantage and conveniently ignores the fact that market strategy requires the existence of both winners and losers. The message has transformed from "not anyone, ever" to "not you, but only if you follow these prescribed steps."
*Student Entrepreneur-Consumers and the Consequences of Lifelong Learning*
Two closely linked market conceptualizations of the higher education student appear to dominate neoliberal discourse: student as consumer and student as entrepreneur. The recasting of students as consumers alters the central mission of higher education; whereas previously education was seen as a process of transformation, it is now one of affirmation (Molesworth et al. 2009). Students go to university to see their beliefs and desires affirmed in a manner similar to the old company adage: "the customer is always right."
Neoliberalism's emphasis on individualism necessitates a second conceptualization of the student as entrepreneur. Students who seek success in life and upward mobility must be more than consumers, they must be producers. Neoliberal logic places an emphasis on the individually-driven acquisition of human capital to make oneself both competitive and productive. As discussed in the previous section on widening participation, aspiration rhetoric situates the burden of one's societal standing on the individual's shoulders. Neoliberalism stresses agency as the driving force of society, and frames government interventions as disruptors rather than facilitators of individual agency. A person's worth is not a passive, inherent trait but rather something that can be actively altered; this project is, at heart, solitary, as each person moves through society making decisions that serve his or her interests. Under this logic, higher education students have been recast as entrepreneurs whose goal is to cultivate and sell the self (Papatsiba 2009). Students thus occupy a position in the market as both producer and good, and the university's mission is transformed from academic instruction to human capital maximization.
Education, as one of the principal means through which people can enhance their human capital, is recast as a lifelong project rather than something that can ever be completed (Kendall 2003). Increasingly, in the United States at least, it appears that the acquisition of bachelor's degrees has become normalized, and employer expectations may in the future undergo a "degree creep." To the extent that students feel pushed into pursuing additional education in order to remain competitive, neoliberalism creates a framework for a sort of bondage, wherein financial institutions in the United States have at their disposal a range of government-backed tools, including wage garnishment, to ensure a return on their investment. Individualist rhetoric offloads responsibility from the state (to create productive citizens) to the individual (to be a productive citizen), and it also offloads the attendant assumption of risk. If a person wanting to increase their human capital enters higher education and either fails or cannot secure a so-called lucrative job, they are nonetheless still on the hook for their failed investment.
While the student loan situation in the United Kingdom as a whole has not devolved to match the student loan debt crisis faced by the United States, the United States functions as a warning of what is in store for UK students as state support to universities and students continues to decrease and tuition continues to increase as a result of the Education Acts of the 1990s and 2000s.
In the United States and, increasingly, the United Kingdom, persons who want to enhance their human capital must take on ever-rising debt loads because personal competitiveness in the job market is linked to education—specifically higher education and degree accumulation. Rising debt loads bind increasing numbers of individuals to financial institutions and render them beholden to them (see Kotz 2008 for a discussion of expanding financialization within neoliberalism). Alternatively, potential students from lower income homes may choose to opt out of higher education and are more likely to forego higher education out of fear of student loan debt (Callendar & Jackson 2005)—the very same group that is often targeted by widening participation initiatives. These trends have occurred alongside the marketization of higher education and the use of internet-based courses by universities to respond to market pressures.
*Marketization and Internet-Based Courses as the Neoliberal Vanguard*
Bound up in the transformation of students into consumers is the transformation of the university from public good to consumer good (Lynch 2006). The marketization of higher education institutions is rooted in the
neoliberal assumption that the market can take over the role of the state in the production of cultural goods (Lynch 2006). Under this view, universities operate as pseudocorporations whose principal project is the distribution of their product (either postsecondary degrees or the added human capital students receive through attendance). As state funding continues to dwindle, universities must locate more efficient ways to distribute their product, and in many ways internet-based education (being both efficient and cost-effective) is the vanguard of the neoliberal transformation of higher education. The consequences and implications of these trends will be explored in this section.
The press for increased participation (discussed in the previous section) has not been accompanied by the requisite increase in funds necessary to handle a burgeoning student load, pressuring universities to divert funds and energy away from teaching and toward the acquisition of industry research grants (Levidow 2002). This "knowledge exchange" is essential for universities in the United Kingdom to cover government-funding shortfall and maintain sustainability (Universities UK 2016). To the extent that universities come to rely on these research grants, they are at risk of becoming beholden to industry interests (Lynch 2006). An attendant risk is that programs deemed unprofitable (particularly arts and humanities programs, but potentially social science programs as well) will lose their standing (Lynch 2006). This risk has perhaps come to fruition in recent years as think pieces regarding the "war on the humanities" in UK higher education occasionally make the media rounds (Preston 2015).
Faced with a growing student load and the need to prioritize research over teaching to cover budget shortfall, universities face pressure to standardize course curricula and create a uniform student experience that does not allow for creative student-teacher interaction and decreases studentteacher face time in general (Levidow 2002). If education is a product, then it makes sense that universities should locate and eliminate inefficiencies in the delivery of that product so that they may deliver it to a greater number of students. The advent and expanded use of internet-based courses could be construed as a consequence of the pressure universities in the United Kingdom and abroad face to maximize student load (Levidow 2002). In addition to its organizational utility in profit maximization, internet-based education is often girded by commercial enterprises through the use of learning management systems such as Blackboard and WebCT (Mullen 2002, Smith & Jeffery 2013).
The expansion of internet-based education is not uniformly negative. Consistent with the aims of widening participation, internet-based educa-
tion has the potential to reach untapped sectors of nontraditional students. Online courses are often structured with a degree of flexibility, which gives students some freedom in choosing where and when to complete course objectives. For nontraditional and working students, online courses can serve as an educational lifeline without which they would be unable to attain a degree. Nonetheless, the expanded use of and reliance on internet-based education poses a potential problem on at least two dimensions (pedagogic and student success), although the research is mixed on the extent to which these concerns bear out.
Although internet-based courses enable universities to take on more students without making costly renovations to physical campus spaces, and although internet-based courses enable instructors to reach a broader swath of students, these conveniences come at the cost of the creative experiences that unfold in classroom settings. Additionally, the tools available to online course creators are heavily skewed toward standardized assessments such as multiple-choice tests, which can be graded automatically. The cost-saving benefit of internet-based courses depreciates with the addition of every course assignment or test that requires a human set of eyes to individually assess every submission. Combined with the quantification of participation through systems that track student access and use (Mullen 2002), students are exposed to a uniform experience that treats them as uniform subjects (see Puzziferro and Shelton 2009 for an extended critique of the assumptions bound up in internet-based education).
Learning management systems such as Blackboard operate as both interface and backdrop; they are the context within which course materials exist, and they are the primary means of interacting with these course materials. They are designed with compatibility and reach in mind and are constrained by the limits and structures of current technology. As a consequence, not just the course itself but the software through which a course is constructed is subject to design considerations that stand apart from any educational project (Mullen 2002).
In the realm of student effects, there is no consensus on the impact of internet-based education on student learning and student success. US-based studies have found performance gaps between students in online courses and traditional courses, with students in online courses performing worse, although the width of the gap varied based on student demographics and course type (Xu & Jaggars 2014). Other studies, however, have found minimal to no difference in student performance when comparing online courses to traditional instruction methods (Rivera & Rice 2002). Yet other studies
have demonstrated superior performance outcomes for students in online courses compared to students in traditional courses (Reasons et al. 2005).
First, it is noteworthy that within this body of literature, there do not appear to be any studies that specifically assess internet-based education outcomes for the types of students that are typically targeted by widening participation initiatives. Whether these students would fare better (due to flexibility) or worse (due to structural disadvantage) is unknown. Second, it is also noteworthy that many of the studies that found positive outcomes for online courses compared to traditional courses looked at online courses that employed subjective assessments (Reasons et al. 2005). If we were to disaggregate online courses that employ creative, subjective assessments and efficiency-based online courses with standardized assessments, it is possible that studies with positive outcomes would fall predominantly into the former camp. The latter camp is more in keeping with the neoliberal push toward efficiency and cost reduction in the market.
Finally, it is also worth noting that internet-based education has been criticized for the pressure it places on educators to be always on as educators, to answer student e-mails at odd hours and to monitor their courses seven days a week (Smith & Jeffery 2013). Although this criticism stands, it is not something unique to internet-based education or perhaps the line between internet-based education and traditional education has blurred considerably in the twenty-first century. For many educators, e-mail serves as the primary means of communication with students. Educators also often post course materials such as lecture slides online. As higher educational culture and student expectations shift in an era of fingertip access, educators will find themselves pulled into a greater reliance on computer technology regardless of one's comfort level and pedagogical disposition. Structural constraints, particularly growing classroom sizes, also place a demand on educators to use e-mail as the principal form of one-on-one interaction with students.
Under neoliberalism's lifelong education ethos, universities are pushed to transform into credential mills; the "student in, student out" mindset frees the university to focus on research and the acquisition of research grants, which it needs to stay afloat in an era of decreasing government subsidies. Internet-based education has its advantages—to the student, to the educator, to the university—but to the extent that it encourages a rigid, standardized student experience, there is little space for critical pedagogy and creative experience, and unprofitable degree programs (often the ones that give voice to disadvantaged groups) are at risk of underfunding.
## **Moving Forward: Future Research**
In the 1980s, Thatcher's regime fell under the influence of the New Right, as social justice initiatives were denigrated and deemed incompatible with free market principles. In spite of this, the push for widening participation in the 1990s employed the rhetoric of equality and correcting imbalances in higher education, although widening participation was justified using the perceived benefits to organizations and institutions as well. The overall effect of widening participation, coupled with government policies that have weakened university and student funding and raised tuition, falls far short of its popularly understood goals, to the point that widening participation could be seen as a tool for social control rather than social justice (Archer 2007). The marketization of higher education institutions and the reformulation of students into entrepreneur-consumers that has accompanied this push for widening participation have both altered the higher education landscape in the United Kingdom. The pressures on universities to maximize student load and minimize cost may lead to the expansion of internet-based education with standardized courses. Researchers in the future will want to examine the impact of internet-based education on the outcomes of students targeted by widening participation initiatives.
Other avenues of research into the effects of neoliberalism on higher education in the United Kingdom include the cooptation and commodification of student and organizational diversity. This research would extend the critical analyses of widening participation in an era where diversity qua diversity is cast as a positive organizational asset. Through individualization and atomization, neoliberalism possesses the capacity to neutralize and even reconfigure social justice aims (Archer 2007, David 2009, Petersen & Davies 2010).
Finally, the recent vote and pending exit of the United Kingdom from the European Union will have broad repercussions for both entities. How that affects higher education and alters the tone and tenor of neoliberal discourse has yet to be determined, but the effects will doubtless be many and varied.
# **Conclusion**
Despite the 2008 economic crisis, neoliberalism has endured as the dominant economic paradigm. While the IMF has since come to argue that neoliberalism has potentially been oversold (Ostroy et al. 2016), trends in marketization and financialization as well as the quasi-reconceptualized aspirational citizen persist. The durability of neoliberalism is likely at-
tributable to many factors, including its adaptable rhetoric (Schmidt & Thatcher 2014). Neoliberal rhetoric obfuscates present conditions with future promises and individualist rhetoric operates as a convenient escape valve that shifts the blame of the struggling working class onto their own shoulders and holds the working class responsible for their own liberation by emphasizing the need for individuals to increase their human capital in order to stay competitive (Harvey 2007).
Today, the average student in the United Kingdom graduates with a higher debt load than in any other English-speaking country; because much of that debt is held by the state, however, UK students are insulated by a number of protections that students in the United States do not have (Kirby 2016). These protections should not be taken for granted. The neoliberal thrust of the past forty years has destabilized higher education's position as public good and has allowed industry forces to gain a measurable foothold within higher education institutions. Individualization and the rhetoric of aspiration have recast UK citizens as private islands who will sink or swim by their own force (or lack) of will. These trends have not gone unchallenged, and some neoliberal projects (such as the construction of the aspirational citizen) face resistance and remain incomplete, but if neoliberalism's flexibility and durability allow it to expand and grow over the next forty years, one can only wonder what that portends for higher education in the United Kingdom.
